tldr: By acquiring an object-aware low-level motion prior via motion-capture imitation that accounts for heavy payload dynamics, and layering a high-level policy constrained within safe operational bounds, humanoids achieve natural, disturbance-resilient bimanual box carrying.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. A library of core motion primitives involving the object is constructed from human motions, and the low-level policy is trained in simulation with the object physically present. The low-level controller is then frozen, and a high-level policy is trained to safely generate task-space commands, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real deployment.
overview:
Enabling humanoid robots to walk and manipulate objects simultaneously—loco-manipulation—is a quintessential challenge in embodied AI. In tasks like bimanual carrying of heavy boxes, object mass and inertia severely disrupt whole-body balance control. Traditionally, hierarchical pipelines pair a whole-body controller (WBC) shaped by manual reward engineering with a downstream task policy. However, these low-level WBCs are typically trained without the manipulated object in the scene, using randomized end-effector force disturbances as a proxy instead. As a result, they fail to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench across the arms and torso, leading to critical breakdowns near the platform's payload limit.

To address this, the authors propose training the low-level controller directly as an "Object-Aware Motion Prior." By placing the physical box inside the simulation scene during motion-capture (MoCap) imitation learning, the robot acquires human-like coordinated coordination while absorbing realistic contact forces at their source. On top of this, a reference-free high-level policy is anchored to the empirical training envelope of the low-level controller, structurally preventing out-of-distribution queries while generalizing the prior across long-horizon multi-stage tasks.

In real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid, a single deployed policy successfully performed box picking, carrying, and placing with payloads up to 7 kg (approaching the robot's torque limits), reactively recovered from intentional mid-carry drops, and handled unseen oversized boxes. In simulation benchmarks, it achieved an 80.7% task success rate, demonstrating far superior robustness and motion naturalness compared to conventional baselines relying on end-effector force approximations.
contributions: Built an object-aware motion prior that absorbs complex multi-contact wrenches by placing the manipulated object directly in the simulation scene during low-level controller training.
Designed a hierarchical interface that geometrically bounds high-level policy actions within the low-level empirical training distribution, preventing motion prior collapse.
Introduced a relative 3D coordinate representation based on the 6 face centers of the box, enabling generalization across significant variations in object geometry and placement.
Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid the carrying of boxes up to a near-limit 7 kg payload and autonomous recovery from mid-carry drops using a single deployed policy.

sections.heading: Why is whole-body humanoid payload carrying so hard?
sections.summary: When carrying heavy objects, object inertia directly affects whole-body balance, making decoupled walking and manipulation infeasible. Existing hierarchical approaches fall short due to object-free force approximations at the low level, a core challenge this paper resolves with an object-aware motion prior.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots operating in human-centric environments, whole-body loco-manipulation is an essential capability. Bimanual box carrying is particularly demanding because the payload's weight and dynamic inertia directly disrupt leg and torso balance, making simple divide-and-conquer schemes—such as developing walking and arm manipulation in isolation and stitching them together—ineffective.

Recent reinforcement learning paradigms generally fall into two categories. One uses end-to-end tracking of human MoCap trajectories, which struggles to generalize beyond the demonstrated reference distribution. The other adopts a hierarchical structure, placing a high-level task policy on top of a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) trained via manual reward engineering. While the latter offers greater versatility, heavy reliance on reward shaping often yields visibly stiff, unnatural motions.

More critically, conventional WBCs are trained without the manipulated object present in the scene. Approximating object dynamics via randomized end-effector force disturbances fails to capture the complex, distributed multi-contact wrenches across the arms and torso when hugging a box. As the payload approaches the robot's physical limits, this simulation-to-reality mismatch becomes catastrophic.

This work tackles contact complexity from the bottom up. By placing the object physically in the simulation during low-level MoCap imitation learning, the robot acquires a motion prior that inherits natural human-like coordination while absorbing realistic contact wrenches at their source. Layering a safely bounded high-level policy on top provides a unified framework to solve long-horizon carrying tasks zero-shot.

sections.heading: Limits of prior work and where this approach stands
sections.summary: Reviewing existing research across whole-body control, motion priors, and legged loco-manipulation highlights how object-aware prior learning and safely bounded hierarchical interfaces overcome conventional weaknesses.
sections.details:
While whole-body control and loco-manipulation have seen extensive study, this work synthesizes their strengths while resolving their respective drawbacks.

### Learning-Based Humanoid Whole-Body Control
Whole-body controllers (WBCs) have been constructed using large-scale imitation learning (such as ExBody and OmniH2O) or manual reward shaping (such as HOMIE and FALCON). However, both paradigms typically omit the manipulated object during training or approximate it using randomized end-effector forces.

### Reusable Motion Priors
Motion priors (or motion primitives), originating in computer animation, are powerful mechanisms for accelerating downstream task learning. While extended to legged robots, existing formulations do not embed object dynamics and often expose abstract latent-space action interfaces that are difficult for downstream task policies to steer.

### Legged Loco-Manipulation
Recent long-horizon loco-manipulation pipelines employ stage-wise reward engineering, dedicated MoCap tracking, or hierarchical setups with pre-trained WBCs. However, reward shaping requires brittle manual tuning, trajectory tracking lacks task flexibility, and traditional hierarchical setups inherit severe physical discrepancies from the low level.

### Positioning of This Work
This work retains a compact, reference-free WBC command interface while executing object-aware MoCap tracking at the low level. By constraining the high-level policy from issuing out-of-distribution queries, it achieves both natural motion and high disturbance rejection during tasks involving sustained, heavy contact wrenches.

sections.heading: Designing the object-aware low level and safe high level
sections.summary: The system couples an object-aware low-level motion prior with a high-level task policy. The low level performs MoCap imitation with the physical object in-scene, while the high level tracks the box's 6 face centers, outputs bounded in-distribution commands, and trains via a finite-state-machine curriculum.
sections.details:
The architecture consists of a two-stage hierarchy: a low-level motion prior policy $\pi^{\mathrm{LL}}$ and an overlying high-level policy $\pi^{\mathrm{HL}}$.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The low-level policy takes proprioceptive observations (joint positions, velocities, etc.) and task-space commands to output target joint positions. The high-level policy receives proprioception, object state information, and coarse target goals to output commands for the low-level controller. Crucially, a transformer mapping $\phi$ structurally restricts high-level commands within the low level's empirical training envelope.

### 3.2 Data Collection and Retargeting
Four core motion primitives are extracted from human MoCap: free walking, carrying walking, box picking, and box placing. To match the Unitree G1 morphology, an interaction-mesh optimization preserves spatial geometric relationships. Data covering three box dimensions (small, medium, large) and multiple orientations yield 30 retargeted clips.

### 3.3 Low-Level Whole-Body Tracking MDP
The low level builds upon the ZEST imitation learning framework. Critically, the physical box is placed in simulation, requiring the policy to track both robot and box motions simultaneously. To prevent out-of-distribution inputs at deployment, the low-level policy itself does not observe the box pose. The command interface is kept compact at 12 dimensions (base height, orientation, linear/angular velocity, and bimanual end-effector positions). Bounded noise is injected into commands during training to ensure tracking stability even under high-level command fluctuations.

### 3.4 High-Level Loco-Manipulation MDP
High-level actions are strictly clipped to the minimum and maximum envelope of the low-level dataset. For box observation, the relative 3D coordinates of the box's six face centers are used, avoiding quaternion singularities and directly representing the surface geometry necessary for grasping.

To facilitate training, a five-phase finite-state scheduler is introduced: (0) Approach, (1) Pick, (2) Carry, (3) Place, and (4) Idle, with normalized phase-dependent rewards. If the box drops mid-carry, a fallback mechanism shifts the state back to Phase 0. Importantly, this scheduler serves purely as training scaffolding; the deployed policy actor never observes phase indices.

### 3.5 Training Setup
Policies are trained using PPO across 8,192 parallel environments in IsaacLab. Extensive domain randomization across robot mass, object mass, friction, and actuator gains enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Real-world limit testing and simulation ablations
sections.summary: Experiments on the Unitree G1 validated payloads up to 7 kg, mid-walk drop recovery, and carrying unseen box sizes. Simulation comparisons substantially outperformed baselines, proving that training with an in-scene object is critical.
sections.details:
The framework was validated through extensive real-robot deployment and large-scale simulation evaluations.

### 4.1 Real-Robot Experiments
A single trained policy was deployed directly on the Unitree G1 without per-trial parameter tuning.

- **Baseline Tasks and Disturbance Recovery**: Smooth approach, pick, carry, and place sequences were achieved with 0.5 kg and 2 kg boxes. When an experimenter forcefully slapped the box out of the robot's hands mid-carry, the robot autonomously transitioned back to approach, re-grasped the box, and completed the delivery. It also re-approached and corrected box placements if the goal box was moved away after placement.
- **Pushing Payload Limits**: The robot carried 5 kg and 7 kg payloads. During 7 kg carries, joint demands neared torque limits, with waist pitch (up to 116.2%), ankle pitch (114.2%), and elbow joints (107.3%) transiently exceeding nominal actuator ratings while maintaining balance. An 8 kg test failed due to grasp slippage, identifying the platform's physical hardware threshold.
- **Unseen Geometries and Elevations**: The policy successfully carried an unseen 60 cm cube (larger than the 54 cm maximum in training), demonstrating the generalization of face-center observations. It also unloaded boxes onto a 75 cm table and picked boxes stacked on cardboard containers.
- **Motion Naturalness**: By imitating human MoCap, the robot avoided unnatural bent-knee crouches or stamping gaits, producing natural, heel-to-toe footfall patterns.

### 4.2 Simulation Evaluation and Ablations
Evaluations across 10,000 simulation environments benchmarked the system.

A monolithic end-to-end baseline achieved only a 3.6% success rate, failing to learn bimanual grasping. An object-free WBC lost balance under heavy loads. A WBC using end-effector force approximations reached a 77.1% success rate but suffered a 78.0% box drop rate. In contrast, the proposed method achieved an 80.7% success rate and recorded the highest motion smoothness.

Ablation studies revealed that removing individual components caused success rates to drop to between 3% and 16%. In particular, removing the in-scene object during low-level training and substituting force approximations collapsed the success rate to 6.7%, confirming that absorbing contact wrenches at the low level is essential.

captions.F2: Joint torque heatmap during lifting and carrying of a heavy 7 kg box. Highlighted in bold red, the waist pitch, ankle pitch, and elbow joints exceed 100% of nominal torque ratings, illustrating that the policy drives the hardware to its operational limits.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: onboard vision and expanding motion repertoires
sections.summary: Current limitations include reliance on external MoCap for object tracking, an inability to execute non-prehensile actions like pushing, and a lack of human subjective evaluations for motion naturalness, pointing toward onboard camera integration.
sections.details:
While the framework shows strong performance, the authors note three primary limitations:

- **Lack of Onboard Perception Integration**: Real-world experiments rely on an external MoCap system for 6-DoF object poses. Achieving full autonomy in unstructured environments requires distilling the policy into a vision-based student model using onboard sensors like depth cameras.
- **Scope of Motion Primitives**: Because the low-level prior is trained on four core primitive families, the high-level policy cannot improvise non-prehensile behaviors—such as pushing objects too heavy to lift—or drastically different grasp modalities. Broadening the task scope requires capturing and retargeting additional human demonstrations.
- **Evaluating Motion Naturalness**: The Naturalness and Smoothness (N&S) index used is an objective physical proxy; rigorous validation of perceived naturalness requires systematic user studies with human observers.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Object-aware hierarchical control for practical humanoids
sections.summary: Combining an object-aware low-level motion prior with a safely bounded high-level policy enables robust, human-like heavy payload carrying on physical humanoids, offering a strong foundation for contact-rich loco-manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for humanoid loco-manipulation, coupling a single-stage object-aware motion prior with a reference-free high-level policy.

By absorbing multi-contact payload wrenches at the low level and structurally constraining high-level commands within the prior's empirical envelope, the framework achieved zero-shot real-world deployment on the Unitree G1. It successfully handled up to 7 kg boxes, recovered from external disturbances, and completed sequential carrying tasks. The approach marks an important milestone, showing that humanoids can maintain human-like motion quality and high physical robustness even under contact-intensive payloads operating near hardware limits.

sections.heading: Appendix: Retargeting and reward formulation details
sections.summary: Key implementation details essential for reproducibility are documented, including MoCap retargeting adjustments, a curriculum for low-level tracking stabilization, and velocity projection reward formulations.
sections.details:
The appendix outlines specific parameters and design choices necessary for reproducing the method.

### Retargeting Adjustments
Uniformly scaling human MoCap data to the Unitree G1 causes foot sliding and end-effector penetration into the box due to differing torso and leg proportions. The authors decouple torso and leg scaling factors and reconstruct kinematic chains anchored to toe ground-contact events.

### Residual Removal Curriculum
The low-level policy outputs joint target offsets added to a feedforward reference. Initially, the reference is set to the demonstration joint angles, but the high-level policy does not supply reference joint angles at deployment. A curriculum gradually shifts the feedforward baseline to the robot's current joint positions over training, improving command-tracking accuracy.

### Velocity Projection Reward
Rather than penalizing pure positional error, the high-level task reward uses a hyperbolic tangent formulation projecting velocity toward the goal: $\hat{r}=\tanh(\alpha \,\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}})$. This provides immediate gradient signals from the onset of movement regardless of distance, preventing aggressive, unnatural acceleration spikes as the robot nears the target.

takeaways: When training low-level controllers for contact-rich tasks, placing the physical object in simulation is essential; randomized force approximations are insufficient.
Physically clipping high-level actions to the low-level empirical training envelope prevents motion prior collapse on unseen tasks.
For box-like objects, observing the relative 3D coordinates of the six face centers provides robustness against geometric variations and eliminates orientation singularities.
Using a hyperbolic tangent velocity projection reward provides consistent gradients and suppresses unnatural aggressive rushes toward goals.
limitations: Real-world trials depend on external optical motion capture for object poses; full autonomy using onboard cameras remains future work.
The system cannot handle behaviors outside its four foundational primitives (such as pushing or rolling heavy payloads).
Motion naturalness was assessed using physical metrics (N&S index) rather than subjective human perceptual studies.
